title: A Mother's Letter to Her Son on the Day He Leaves Home
author: Katherine Martinko
summary: In this personal essay, parenting writer Katherine Martinko marks her son's departure for a year abroad in Japan with a reflective letter surveying seventeen years of motherhood, from a reluctant, unplanned pregnancy at twenty-one through the accumulated small labors of child-raising to this final threshold moment. The piece is structured as a list of parting advice, live authentically rather than for an audience, choose compassion over speculation, trust intuition, stay present rather than distracted, say yes to experiences, read rather than scroll, and choose companions of good character. Running beneath the advice is Martinko's recurring theme, developed at length in her forthcoming book on phone-free parenting, that attention and presence are the scarcest resources of modern family life, and that a childhood spent teaching a child to notice the world rather than perform it for an audience is itself the parenting project. The essay closes on the bittersweet arithmetic of parenting: the years felt endless while they were happening and vanished the moment they were over.
points: Martinko frames seventeen years of parenting as an arithmetic of slow accumulation followed by sudden ending, arguing that the felt duration of child-raising and its actual brevity are two entirely different kinds of time.

Her central piece of advice, 'live your life; don't perform it,' extends her broader public argument (developed in her upcoming book Hold the Phone) that social-media performance corrodes the authenticity of lived experience, particularly for young people.

She distinguishes moral seriousness from moralizing by grounding advice in personal admission, her own reluctant, unplanned entry into motherhood, rather than presenting herself as a parenting authority handing down rules.
The letter treats attentiveness itself as a moral practice, not just a productivity habit, quoting Mary Oliver to frame 'paying attention' as an ethical obligation to both self and others.
Endorsements from Jonathan Haidt and Anna Lembke embedded in the newsletter situate this personal essay within Martinko's larger public project on childhood, smartphones, and parental agency.
quotes: Exactly 17 years, 2 weeks, and 1 day after I brought you home from the midwifery clinic in Toronto, a screaming, red-faced, shrivelled little human, we have reached the end of your childhood.
Then you were my baby. Now you are my child." The next part was left unsaid, but I can hear it in my head. "Eventually, you will be a man.
Live your life; don't perform it. It's tempting to do things for an online audience, and even to select activities based on their potential appeal for social media posts, but resist that urge.
Err on the side of compassion. You never know what a person is dealing with, what burdens they might be carrying, what sort of awful day they may have had.
Mary Oliver wrote, "To pay attention, this is our endless and proper work." Do that. Do it for yourself, do it for others. Give them the gift of your full attention.
Books will make you smarter than anything; they will expose you to challenging new ideas that require you to sit with your thoughts and contemplate the world, as humans have done for millennia.

I've revelled in raising you for 17 years, but now I have to let you go, pretty much as far away as it's physically possible to go! I will miss you so much, but seeing how excited you are to venture out into the world makes it easier to say goodbye.
